rows.title: There are 140,000 job openings in Colorado. Here are a handful of them.
rows.standfirst: Out-of-work Coloradans are having a more challenging time finding a job, as employers have also cut back due to economic uncertainty. But there are still companies hiring.

rows.title: The special session change to Colorado’s tax code that will most affect small businesses
rows.standfirst: Colorado’s so-called sales tax vendor fee is being shut off next year to generate about $57 million in new tax revenue each year

rows.title: Pueblo County to President Trump: Keep our coal-burning Comanche Station making power indefinitely
rows.standfirst: Big economic impacts are on the line as Xcel transitions from generating power at the expensive and unreliable Comanche Unit 3. The county wonders if its citizens are being punished for twice voting for Donald Trump.

rows.title: Self-driving car company Waymo heading to metro Denver in 2026
rows.standfirst: Customer rides won’t start immediately as “exploratory phase” is conducted. A dozen autonomous vehicles will be training in the Denver metro first.

rows.title: Trump tariffs on Colorado businesses are effectively “7 to 8 times higher” than last year, state report says
rows.standfirst: Gov. Polis asked for a deep dive into the impact of the higher, reciprocal tariffs on the state’s economy. The report concluded there will be “worse economic outcomes.”

rows.title: Did the CEO of a Colorado-based corporation earn nearly $7B in 2024?
rows.standfirst: Yes. Alexander Karp, CEO of the Colorado-based data firm Palantir, received $6.8 billion in 2024, including salary and stock value changes.

rows.title: Pueblo County commissioners spar over message to Trump, but agree the “just transition” from coal-fired power feels unfair
rows.standfirst: Colorado utilities regulators will look again at a community proposal to replace coal power with gas or small modular nuclear reactors at Comanche Station

rows.title: Planned closure of The Limon Leader would leave another “news desert” on Colorado’s Eastern Plains
rows.standfirst: If The Limon Leader weekly newspaper shuts down by the end of the year as planned, Lincoln County would no longer have a dedicated local news source.

rows.title: What’s Working: Aging in Colorado is expensive. Here’s what’s being done about it
rows.standfirst: Advocates for more affordable aging are growing and official state listening sessions start this month

rows.title: How to treat a river: Reshaping the Arkansas River into a Colorado success after a century of abuse
rows.standfirst: From the high headwaters all the way to the state line, people who care are trying to redeem a hard-working stream

rows.title: EchoStar unloads wireless spectrum to Musk’s SpaceX for $17 billion
rows.standfirst: The Douglas County satellite technology company, which also operates Dish Network, is also selling off wireless spectrum to AT&T

rows.title: PNC to buy FirstBank for $4.1B, expanding to Arizona, Colorado
rows.standfirst: The Lakewood-based FirstBank operates 120 retail branches with $26.7 billion in assets

rows.title: Cañon City’s latest setback to finally getting a community swimming pool: Angry business owners
rows.standfirst: A tax on “amusements” in the Southern Colorado city on the ballot this fall has the Royal Gorge railroad threatening “costly legal fight”

rows.title: How a little help desk inside a Denver community center is preventing homelessness
rows.standfirst: Elevated Denver purposely put the Westwood help desk in a spot with no stigma, next to a library branch and fitness classes

rows.title: Colorado awards Amazon $25.4 million to provide satellite internet to areas with poor service
rows.standfirst: Amazon also captured 44% of the state’s locations with poor internet service. With two-thirds of states submitting final BEAD proposals by deadline, Colorado ranks 2nd highest so far for share of awards to satellite providers Amazon or Starlink.

rows.title: Xcel Energy plans to sell water it once held for power production to Lower Arkansas River farmers
rows.standfirst: The deal, which could be worth more than $44 million, includes Colorado Springs Utilities and is expected to close early next year

rows.title: Will Colorado lose 30,000 jobs when Space Command moves to Alabama?
rows.standfirst: No. Only 1,700 employees are assigned to the Colorado Springs-based Space Command headquarters, which is set to move to Huntsville, Ala.

rows.title: What’s Working: Colorado Startup Week debuts in Front Range to reignite founder fever
rows.standfirst: You may recognize its old name, Denver Startup Week. Organizers are leaning into the entrepreneurial community beyond Denver.

rows.title: 7 Colorado counties plan to ask voters to double or triple lodging taxes to pay for roads, police
rows.standfirst: Chaffee, Custer, Eagle, Gilpin, Routt, Ouray and Park counties hope voters will approve increased lodging taxes — allowed under new legislation — to pay for budget shortfalls

rows.title: Small modular nuclear reactors are having a moment. Will they arrive in time for Pueblo?
rows.standfirst: The feds, the state, cities, counties, companies and even Denver’s airport are looking at clean, nuclear power. The problem is, no small modular reactors have been built in the US.

rows.title: Colorado’s Republican US representatives decline to fight Trump on Space Command, even as they risk voter fallout
rows.standfirst: If they cross Trump, Colorado’s Republican members of Congress risk political consequences — lost endorsements, primary challengers, fewer campaign donations — but they also could put future federal projects in jeopardy

rows.title: Project introducing rye to drought-stricken San Luis Valley aims to build agricultural resilience
rows.standfirst: The Rye Resurgence Project partners producers and local businesses to grow a sustainable crop that uses less water and creates new markets to support San Luis Valley farms

rows.title: Waymo’s autonomous cars are testing on Denver streets. Are rides to the airport in the future?
rows.standfirst: The driverless ride service is expected to launch service in 2026. DEN officials are ready to work with Waymo to get service to the airport

rows.title: Do Colorado cities pay to have restaurants reviewed for the Michelin Guide?
rows.standfirst: Yes. The Colorado Tourism Office, along with tourism boards in Denver and other cities, have paid to bring Michelin inspectors to cities.

rows.title: What’s Working: While AI and quantum were big attractions, Colorado Startup Week was about founders
rows.standfirst: Plus: Techstars Boulder shares its relaunch plans, data on tech startups in Denver, Colorado unemployment rate falls to 4.2%, more!

rows.title: If a renter dies in Colorado, can their relatives be fined for a broken lease?
rows.standfirst: No. Landlords cannot fine the families of deceased tenants in Colorado under a law that went into effect Sept. 1.

rows.title: Colorado lawmakers outlawed some apartment fees. Now small businesses want protections, too.
rows.standfirst: The Colorado legislature banned CAM fees in residential leases starting Jan. 1.

rows.title: The Colorado legislature just tackled two budget crises. Another is on the horizon.
rows.standfirst: Providing the same level of government programs and services next fiscal year is predicted to cost $850 million more than the legislature will have available to spend

rows.title: Did Xcel Energy help spark the Marshall fire? Plaintiffs will push for answers in Boulder County trial.
rows.standfirst: More than 300 lawsuits on behalf of roughly 4,000 plaintiffs were consolidated into a case being heard in Boulder District Court. Jury selection starts Thursday.

rows.title: What will happen to the US patent office in Denver as its regional director leaves?
rows.standfirst: Molly Kocialski left after a decade promoting patents and innovation in the nine-state Rocky Mountain region. The Denver office was the second regional office outside of D.C.

rows.title: What’s Working: A Colorado firm struggling to hire staff has no job openings — and that’s the new plan
rows.standfirst: It’s an effort to rethink how to find and hire employees who can be the best fit eventually, Mineralife says. Plus: One open job for every unemployed Coloradan, readers on the economy and more!
